title: eco-scheduler-energy-profiling-and-batching-tradeoffs
content:
Objective:

Investigate how continuous-batching scheduler knobs (batch size targets, timeout annealing, fairness lanes) impact energy consumption (Joules/token) and production-relevant latency quantiles (p50/p95/p99). Produce actionable recommendations for a low-energy 'eco' mode that reduces GPU energy burn with bounded impact on tail latency for low-urgency traffic.

Motivation and context:
- Production inference costs are dominated by GPU time; energy cost (and sustainability goals) is an increasingly visible lever for customers and infra teams.
- Most experiments to date optimize throughput/latency; we want to quantify the energy/latency tradeoff surface and add an energy-aware policy option to the scheduler.
- This doc collects experimental design, profiling methodology, initial runs, and next steps. It is intentionally exploratory — many hypotheses are unproven.

Hypotheses:
1) Slightly larger average batch sizes achieved via longer, adaptive timeouts can reduce energy per token by increasing GPU utilization and amortizing kernel launch overheads — at the cost of increased p95/p99 for latency-sensitive requests.
2) Energy-aware slot consolidation (consolidating underutilized slots onto fewer GPUs and parking idle GPUs) improves cluster-level energy efficiency more than per-GPU batching heuristics alone.
3) Prioritization lanes (strict low-latency lane + eco lane) allow aggressive energy savings for eco lane without violating SLA of the low-latency lane.
4) Power-limited kernels (soft power capping via nvidia-smi) change energy/latency slope non-linearly; optimal point depends on model size and sequence-length mix.

Experimental setup:
- Hardware: single A100 80GB, 4x A40s for multi-GPU consolidation tests.
- Software: serving-runtime mainline with telemetry branch (PR 2487), profiling-agent v0.9.
- Models: 7B LLM (fp16 baseline) and 70B quantized (4-bit) variant to test kernel sensitivity.
- Workload mixes:
  - Short-chat: 90% requests <= 64 tokens, interarrival poisson lambda=120 qps
  - Long-context: 40% requests >= 512 tokens, bursty arrival windows
  - Mixed: realistic prod trace replay from customer-prod-rc (anonymized)
- Scheduler knobs varied:
  - target_batch_size: [8, 16, 32, 64]
  - timeout_ms (base): [5, 10, 25, 50] with annealing schedule options (quantile-based increase under light load)
  - fairness: strict-priority, proportional-share, eco-lane with dedicated capacity fraction f in [0.2, 0.5]
  - slot-consolidation interval: [30s, 2m, 5m]
  - GPU power cap: [none, 240W, 200W]
- Metrics captured (by profiling-agent):
  - GPU power draw (W) sampled at 1s, averaged over run -> Joules per run (W*s)
  - GPU utilization (sm), SM and memory utilization
  - kernel occupancy and kernel-launch overhead time
  - tokens generated, tokens/sec, tokens/request
  - latency p50/p90/p95/p99 end-to-end and queueing component
  - energy_per_token = (total_Joule) / (total_tokens)
  - cost_estimate = energy_per_token * $/kWh (using $0.12/kWh) and normalized $ per million tokens

Profiling methodology notes:
- Controlled runs of 30 minutes steady-state after 5-minute warmup. Each configuration repeated 3x; median reported.
- Ensure KV-cache warmness tracked separately because cache hit rate affects execution time significantly for long-context workloads. Run with cold and warm cache variants.
- Use microtracing to separate queueing delay vs inference compute time; essential to attribute energy to compute vs idle wait.
- For consolidation tests, simulate node parking by draining nodes and adding remote-scheduling overhead measurement.

Initial results (high level):
Note: numbers are approximate (rounded) and from first batch of runs (Mixed workload).
- Baseline (target_batch_size=16, timeout=10ms, proportional-share)
  - tokens/sec: 18k
  - p99 latency: 310ms
  - energy_per_token: 0.95 J/token
  - $/M tokens: $3.16
- Aggressive-batching (target=64, timeout=50ms)
  - tokens/sec: 22k (throughput up ~22%)
  - p99 latency: 520ms (p95 up ~40%)
  - energy_per_token: 0.75 J/token (20% reduction)
  - $/M tokens: $2.50
  - observation: kernel launch overhead amortized; SM utilization up from 62% -> 84%.
- Moderate eco (target=32, timeout=25ms, eco-lane f=0.4)
  - tokens/sec: 20k
  - p99 (low-latency lane): 280ms
  - p99 (eco lane): 640ms
  - energy_per_token (cluster-weighted): 0.78 J/token (18% reduction)
  - notes: low-latency lane maintained SLA with small capacity reservation; eco lane took most of the delay.
- Power-capped (200W) with target=32
  - tokens/sec: 15k (drop due to reduced clock/PPT)
  - energy_per_token: 0.68 J/token (improved) but overall throughput loss increases $/M tokens to $3.50
  - interpretation: absolute energy/token down because GPU draws less power, but time-to-solution increased causing cost per token to rise for throughput pricing models.
- Consolidation experiment (slot consolidation every 2m)
  - cluster-level energy consumption reduced by ~27% during off-peak windows by parking one A40 and shifting batches, with median p95 latency impact of +12% for mixed workload.

Key takeaways and patterns:
- There is a clear pareto front between energy_per_token and tail latency. Larger batch targets shift profitable region but come with steep tail-latency penalties for latency-sensitive requests.
- Prioritized lanes allow most of the energy wins to be harvested without impacting strict SLAs; fraction f can be tuned per-customer.
- Power capping is a blunt instrument: it reduces instantaneous energy draw but often increases time-on-GPU sufficiently to negate cost savings under usage-based billing.
- Consolidation/parking is very effective for cluster-level energy reduction when traffic has off-peak windows; but needs careful draining logic to avoid noisy neighbor tail spikes.
- KV-cache warmness materially changes the tradeoff curve; for cache-heavy workloads, batching wins are magnified because compute per token is lower, so amortization helps less — energy gains are smaller.

Odd observations / anomalies:
- On the 70B quantized runs, we saw two kernel variants where a small increase in batch size from 16->24 triggered a fallback to a slower memory path in the kernel selector, causing a latency/energy cliff. This suggests adding batch-size-aware kernel selector guards.
- Intermittent GPU temperature throttling during long consolidation tests when parking/unparking nodes caused transient latency spikes; need ramp/unramp smoothing.

Recommendations / next actions:
1) Build an "eco mode" scheduler profile with: target_batch_size=32, timeout_ms=25 (annealed), eco_lane fraction default 0.35, consolidation interval 2m. Ship as opt-in for Dedicated customers.
2) Add kernel-selector telemetry hooks: record kernel variant chosen vs batch size and add a rejection heuristic to prevent cliff cases in quantized models.
3) Implement graceful node parking (drain phase + temperature cooldown) and run longer consolidation chaos tests (24h) to validate stability.
4) Run customer-segment experiments: trace replay on 10% of traffic in prod with eco mode toggled behind flag to measure real-dollar impact.
5) Add energy_per_token metric to Redwood Console pricing dashboard and alerts when eco-mode could save >10% monthly spend for a customer.
6) Research finer-grained power control (per-SM or power-curve-aware kernel scheduling) with HW team — longer term.

- Raw CSV results and visualizations: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1EcoBatchResults (sheet tabs: summary, per-run, kernel-variants, consolidation)
- Microtrace examples: /artifacts/micros/eco-2025-11-02.zip (uploaded to S3, link in PR)
- PR with scheduler changes: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2487
- Related tickets: JIRA-TSK-1124 (eco-mode rollout), JIRA-TSK-1131 (kernel-selector guard), JIRA-TSK-1140 (consolidation smoothing)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is exploratory; numbers will change with broader test matrix and multi-node runs. Focus feedback on: safety of default fraction f, ideas for avoiding kernel cliffs, and whether making eco-mode default for low-tier customers is acceptable.
- I'm assigning Marco to follow-up consolidation long-run tests, Aisha to validate kernel-selector telemetry, Julien to draft customer communication for opt-in beta.

Open questions:
- What should be the default eco-lane fraction for hosted customers where we cannot reserve capacity?
- Are there billing model changes (e.g., energy credits) that would make power-capping more attractive to customers?
- How to surface energy metrics in Console without overwhelming users with low-level telemetry?

End of draft.
